{{Short description|Two-dimensional laminar boundary layer that forms on a semi-infinite plate}}
In [[physics]] and [[fluid mechanics]], a '''Blasius boundary layer''' (named after [[Paul Richard Heinrich Blasius]]) describes the steady two-dimensional laminar [[boundary layer]] that forms on a semi-infinite plate which is held parallel to a constant unidirectional flow. Falkner and Skan later generalized Blasius' solution to wedge flow ([[Falkner–Skan boundary layer]]), i.e. flows in which the plate is not parallel to the flow.

==Prandtl's boundary layer equations==

[[Image:Blasius1.PNG|thumb|right|300px|A [[schematic]] diagram of the Blasius flow profile. The streamwise velocity component <math>u(\eta)/U</math> is shown, as a function of the similarity variable <math>\eta</math>.]]

Using scaling arguments, [[Ludwig Prandtl]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Prandtl|first1=L.|title=Über Flüssigkeitsbewegung bei sehr kleiner Reibung|journal=Verhandlinger 3. Int. Math. Kongr. Heidelberg|date=1904|pages=484–491}}</ref> argued that about half of the terms in the [[Navier-Stokes equations]] are negligible in boundary layer flows (except in a small region near the leading edge of the plate). This leads to a reduced set of equations known as the [[Boundary layer#Boundary layer equations|boundary layer equations]]. For steady [[incompressible flow]] with constant viscosity and density, these read:

* Mass Continuity: <math> \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y} = 0 </math>
* <math>x</math>-Momentum: <math> u \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = - \dfrac{1}{\rho} \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial x} + {\nu} \dfrac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} </math>
* <math>y</math>-Momentum: <math> 0 = -  \dfrac{\partial p}{\partial y}  </math>

Here the coordinate system is chosen with <math>x</math> pointing parallel to the plate in the direction of the flow and the <math>y</math> coordinate pointing normal to the plate, <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> velocity components, <math>p</math> is the [[pressure]], <math>\rho</math> is the [[density]] and <math>\nu</math> is the [[viscosity|kinematic viscosity]].

A number of similarity solutions to this set of equations have been found for various types of flow, including flow on a thin flat-plate. The term ''similarity'' refers to the property that the velocity profiles at different positions in the flow are the same apart from scaling factors. Similarity scaling factors reduce the set of partial differential equations to a relatively easily solved set of non-linear ordinary differential equations. [[Paul Richard Heinrich Blasius]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Blasius|first1=H.|title=Grenzschichten in Flüssigkeiten mit kleiner Reibung|journal=Z. Angew. Math. Phys.|date=1908|volume=56|pages=1–37}}</ref> one of Prandtl's students, developed the similarity model corresponding to the flow for the case where the [[pressure gradient]], <math>{\partial p}</math>/<math>{\partial x}</math>, along a thin flat-plate is negligible compared to any pressure gradient in the boundary layer region.

==Blasius equation - first-order boundary layer==

Blasius showed that for the case where <math>{\partial p}/{\partial x} = 0</math>, the Prandtl <math>x</math>-momentum equation has a [[self-similar solution]]. The self-similar solution exists because the equations and the boundary conditions are invariant under the transformation

<math display="block">x\rightarrow c^2 x, \quad y\rightarrow cy, \quad u\rightarrow u, \quad v\rightarrow \frac{v}{c}</math>

where <math>c</math> is any positive constant. He introduced the self-similar variables

[[File:Blasius.png|thumb|Developing Blasius boundary layer (not to scale). The velocity profile <math>f'</math> is shown in red at selected positions along the plate. The blue lines represent, in top to bottom order, the 99% free stream velocity line (<math>\delta_{99\%}, \eta\approx 5.29</math>), the displacement thickness (<math>\delta_*, \eta \approx 1.79</math>) and <math>\delta(x)</math> (<math>\eta = 1.51</math>). See [[Boundary layer thickness]] for a more detailed explanation.]]

<math display="block"> \eta = \dfrac{y}{\delta(x)} = y \sqrt{ \dfrac{U}{\nu x} }, \quad  \psi = \sqrt{\nu U x} f(\eta) </math>

where <math display="inline"> \delta(x) \propto \sqrt{  \nu x / U} </math> is the [[boundary layer thickness]], <math>U</math> is the free stream velocity, and <math>\psi</math> is the [[stream function]].  The stream function is directly proportional to the normalized function, <math> f(\eta) </math>, which is only a function of the similarity thickness variable. This leads directly to the velocity components:<ref>Schlichting, H., (1979). ''Boundary-Layer Theory'', 7th ed., McGraw-Hill, New York.</ref>{{rp|p=136}}

<math display="block"> u(x,y) =   \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} = U f'(\eta), \quad v(x,y) = - \dfrac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{\nu U}{x}} [ \eta f'(\eta) - f(\eta)]  </math>

Where the prime denotes differentiation with respect to <math> \eta </math>.
Substitution into the <math>x</math>-momentum equation gives the Blasius equation

<math display="block"> 2f^{(3)} + f'' f = 0 </math>

The boundary conditions are the [[no-slip condition]], the impermeability of the wall and the free stream velocity outside the boundary layer

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 u(x,0) &= 0 &\rightarrow&& f'(0) &= 0 \\
 v(x,0) &= 0 &\rightarrow&& f(0) &= 0 \\
 u(x,\infty) &= U &\rightarrow&& f'(\infty) &= 1
\end{align} </math>

This is a third-order non-linear [[ordinary differential equation]] which can be solved numerically, e.g. with the [[shooting method]]. The boundary condition at infinity is converted to <math>f''(0) = 0.332043934904293</math>.

With the solution for <math>f</math> and its derivatives in hand, the Prandtl <math>y</math>-momentum equation can be non-dimensionalized and rearranged to obtain the <math>y</math>-pressure gradient, <math>{\partial p}</math>/<math>{\partial y}</math>, as<ref name=Weyburne>
{{cite book
 | last = Weyburne | first = David 
 | title = Aspects of Boundary Layer Theory
 | date = 2022
 | isbn = 978-0-578-98334-9 }}
</ref>{{rp|p=46}}

<math display="block"> \frac{{x^2 }}{{U^2 \delta^* }}\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{{\partial P}}{{\partial y}}\quad  = \quad \frac{1}{2} \eta f^{(3)}\; + \;\frac{1}{2}f''\; - \;\frac{1}{4}ff'\; + \;\frac{1}{4}\eta f'^2 \; + \;\frac{1}{4}\eta f f'' \quad ,</math>
where <math>\delta^*</math> is the Blasius displacement thickness.

The Blasius normal velocity <math>v(x,y)</math> and the <math>y</math>-pressure gradient asymptotes to a value of 0.86 and 0.43, respectively, at large <math>\eta</math>-values whereas <math>u(x,y)</math> asymptotes to the free stream velocity <math>U</math>.  As <math>\eta</math> goes to zero, the scaled <math>y</math>-pressure gradient goes to 0.16603.

[[File:Graph Blasius velocities and y-pressure gradient versus normal height above wall.png|thumb|right|300px|A schematic depiction of the scaled velocities and <math>y</math>-pressure gradient for Blasius boundary layer flow versus the scaled normal height above the wall, <math>\eta</math>.  The red line is the Blasius scaled velocity <math>u(x,y)/U</math>, the green line is the Blasius <math display="inline">v(x,y)/\sqrt{\nu U/x}</math> and the blue line is the Blasius <math>\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{{dP}}{{dy}}/\sqrt{\nu U^3/x^3}</math>.]]

The limiting form for small <math>\eta \ll 1</math> is

<math display="block"> f(\eta) =  \frac{1}{2}\alpha \eta^2 + O(\eta^5), \qquad \alpha = 0.332057336215196  </math>

and the limiting form for large <math>\eta \gg 1</math> is<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Boyd|first1=J.|title=The Blasius function: computations before computers, the value of tricks, undergraduate projects, and open research problems | journal=SIAM Rev.|date=2008 |volume=50 |issue=4 |pages=791–804|doi=10.1137/070681594 |bibcode=2008SIAMR..50..791B }}</ref>

<math display="block"> f(\eta) = \eta - \beta + O\left((\eta-\beta)^{-2} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\eta-\beta)^2}\right), \qquad \beta =1.7207876575205  </math>

The characteristic parameters for boundary layers are the two sigma viscous boundary layer thickness,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weyburne|first1=D.|title=New thickness and shape parameters for the boundary layer velocity profile |journal=Experimental Thermal and Fluid Science|date=2014|volume=54|pages=22–28|doi=10.1016/j.expthermflusci.2014.01.008 }}</ref> <math>\delta_v</math>, the displacement thickness <math>\delta^*</math>, the momentum thickness <math>\theta</math>, the wall [[shear stress]] <math>\tau_w</math> and the drag force <math>F</math> acting on a length <math>l</math> of the plate.  For the Blasius solution, they are given by
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\delta_{99} &\approx \delta_v = 5.29 \sqrt{\frac{\nu x}{U}} \\[1ex]
\delta^* &= \delta_1 = \int_0^\infty \left(1-\frac{u}{U} \right) dy =  1.72 \sqrt{\frac{\nu x}{U}} \\[1ex]
\theta &= \delta_2 = \int_0^\infty \frac{u}{U}\left(1-\frac{u}{U} \right) dy =  0.665 \sqrt{\frac{\nu x}{U}} \\[1ex]
\tau_w &= \mu \left.\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} =  0.332 \sqrt{\frac{\rho\mu U^3}{x}} \\[1ex]
F &= 2 \int_0^l \tau_w dx =  1.328 \sqrt{\rho\mu l U^3}
\end{align}</math>

The factor <math>2</math> in the drag force formula is to account both sides of the plate.

The [[Boundary layer|Von Kármán Momentum integral]] and the energy integral for Blasius profile reduce to

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\frac{\tau_w}{\rho U^2} &= \frac{\partial \delta_2}{\partial x} + \frac{v_w}{U} \\
\frac{2\varepsilon}{\rho U^3} &= \frac{\partial \delta_3}{\partial x} + \frac{v_w}{U}
\end{align}</math>

where <math>\tau_w</math> is the wall shear stress, <math>v_w</math> is the wall injection/suction velocity, <math>\varepsilon</math> is the energy dissipation rate, <math>\delta_2</math> is the momentum thickness and <math>\delta_3</math> is the energy thickness.

===Uniqueness of Blasius solution===
The Blasius solution is not unique from a mathematical perspective,<ref name=VanDyke>
{{cite book
 | last = Van Dyke | first = Milton | author-link = Milton Van Dyke
 | title = Perturbation methods in fluid mechanics
 | publisher = Parabolic Press
 | date = 1975
 | isbn = 9780915760015 }}
</ref>{{rp|p=131}} as [[Ludwig Prandtl]] himself noted it in his [[Boundary layer|transposition theorem]] and analyzed by series of researchers such as [[Keith Stewartson]], [[Paul A. Libby]].<ref>Libby, Paul A., and Herbert Fox. "Some perturbation solutions in laminar boundary-layer theory." Journal of Fluid Mechanics 17.3 (1963): 433-449.</ref> To this solution, any one of the infinite discrete set of eigenfunctions can be added, each of which satisfies the linearly perturbed equation with homogeneous conditions and [[exponential decay]] at infinity. The first of these eigenfunctions turns out to be the <math>x</math> derivative of the first order Blasius solution, which represents the uncertainty in the effective location of the origin.

===Second-order boundary layer===
This boundary layer approximation predicts a non-zero vertical velocity far away from the wall, which needs to be accounted in next order outer inviscid layer and the corresponding inner boundary layer solution, which in turn will predict a new vertical velocity and so on. The vertical velocity at infinity for the first order boundary layer problem from the Blasius equation is

<math display="block"> v = 0.86 \sqrt{\frac{\nu U}{x}}</math>

The solution for second order boundary layer is zero. The solution for outer inviscid and inner boundary layer are<ref name="VanDyke"/>{{rp|p=134}}

<math display="block">\psi(x,y) \sim \begin{cases}
    y - \sqrt{\frac{\nu}{Ux}} \beta \ \Re \sqrt{x+iy},& \text{outer } \\
    \sqrt{\nu Ux} f(\eta)  + 0,              & \text{inner} 
\end{cases}</math>

Again as in the first order boundary problem, any one of the infinite set of eigensolution can be added to this solution. In all the solutions <math>Re = Ux/\nu</math> can be considered as a [[Reynolds number]].

===Third-order boundary layer===

Since the second order inner problem is zero, the corresponding corrections to third order problem is null i.e., the third order outer problem is same as second order outer problem.<ref name="VanDyke"/>{{rp|p=139}} The solution for third-order correction does not have an exact expression, but the inner boundary layer expansion is of the form,

<math display="block">\psi(x,y) \sim \sqrt{2\nu Ux} f(\eta)  + 0 + \left(\frac{\nu}{Ux}\right)^{3/2} \left[\log \left(\frac{Ux}{\nu}\right) \sqrt{\frac{x}{2}}  f_{32}(\eta) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2x}} f_{31}(\eta) \right] + \cdot\cdot\cdot</math>

where <math>f_{32}</math> is the first eigensolution of the first order boundary layer solution (which is <math>x</math> derivative of the first order Blasius solution) and solution for <math>f_{31}</math> is nonunique and the problem is left with an undetermined constant.

==Blasius boundary layer with suction==
Suction is one of the common methods to postpone the boundary layer separation.<ref>Rosenhead, Louis, ed. Laminar boundary layers. Clarendon Press, 1963.</ref> Consider a uniform suction velocity at the wall <math>v(0)=-V</math>.  [[Bryan Thwaites]]<ref>Thwaites, Bryan. On certain types of boundary-layer flow with continuous surface suction. HM Stationery Office, 1946.</ref> showed that the solution for this problem is same as the Blasius solution without suction for distances very close to the leading edge. Introducing the transformation

<math display="block">\psi = \sqrt{2 U \nu x} f(\xi,\eta), \quad \xi = V\sqrt{\frac{x}{2U\nu}}, \quad \eta = \sqrt{\frac{U}{2\nu x}}y</math>

into the boundary layer equations leads to

<math display="block"> u = U \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta}, \quad v = - \sqrt{\frac{U\nu}{2x}} \left(f + \xi \frac{\partial f}{\partial \xi} - \eta \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta} \right),</math>
<math display="block">\frac{\partial^3 f}{\partial \eta^3} + f \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \eta^2} + \xi \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial \xi} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \eta^2} - \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \xi\partial \eta} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta} \right) =0</math>

with boundary conditions,

<math display="block">f(\xi,0) =\xi, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta}(\xi,0) =0, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta}(\xi,\infty)=0.</math>

===Von Mises transformation===

Iglisch obtained the complete numerical solution in 1944.<ref>Iglisch, Rudolf. Exakte Berechnung der laminaren Grenzschicht an der längsangeströmten ebenen Platte mit homogener Absaugung. Oldenbourg, 1944.</ref> If further [[Richard von Mises|von Mises]] transformation<ref>Von Mises, Richard. "Bemerkungen zur hydrodynamik." Z. Angew. Math. Mech 7 (1927): 425-429.</ref> is introduced

<math display="block"> \sigma = 2\xi, \quad \psi-Vx = \frac{U\nu}{2V} \sigma \tau^2, \quad \phi = \frac{4u^2}{U^2}, \quad \chi = U^2-u^2 = U^2\left(1-\frac{V}{4} \right), </math>

then the equations become

<math display="block">\sqrt{\phi} \frac{\partial ^2 \phi}{\partial \tau^2} + \left(2\sigma\tau +\tau^3 - \frac{\sqrt{\phi}}{\tau} \right) \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \tau} = 2\sigma \tau^2 \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial \sigma}</math>

with boundary conditions,

<math display="block">\phi(0,\tau)=4, \quad \phi(\sigma,0)=0, \quad \phi(\sigma,\infty)=4.</math>

This [[parabolic partial differential equation]] can be marched starting from <math>\sigma=0</math> numerically.

===Asymptotic suction profile===

Since the convection due to suction and the diffusion due to the solid wall are acting in the opposite direction, the profile will reach steady solution at large distance, unlike the Blasius profile where boundary layer grows indefinitely. The solution was first obtained by [[Alan Arnold Griffith|Griffith]] and [[F.W. Meredith]].<ref>Griffith, A. A., and F. W. Meredith. "The possible improvement in aircraft performance due to the use of boundary layer suction." Royal Aircraft Establishment Report No. E 3501 (1936): 12.</ref> For  distances from the leading edge of the plate <math>x\gg \nu U/V^2</math>, both the boundary layer thickness and the solution are independent of <math>x</math> given by

<math display="block"> \delta = \frac{\nu}{V}, \quad u = U(1-e^{-yV/\nu}), \quad v = -V.</math>

[[Keith Stewartson|Stewartson]]<ref>Stewartson, K. "On asymptotic expansions in the theory of boundary layers." Studies in Applied Mathematics 36.1-4 (1957): 173-191.</ref> studied matching of full solution to the asymptotic suction profile.

==Compressible Blasius boundary layer==

Here Blasius boundary layer with a specified [[specific enthalpy]] <math>h</math> at the wall is studied. The [[density]] <math>\rho</math>, [[viscosity]] <math>\mu</math> and thermal conductivity <math>\kappa</math> are no longer constant here. The equation for conservation of mass, momentum and energy become

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\frac{\partial (\rho u)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (\rho v)}{\partial y} & = 0,\\
\rho \left(u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} \right) & = \frac{\partial }{\partial y} \left(\mu\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right),\\
\rho \left(u \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \right) &=  \frac{\partial }{\partial y} \left(\frac{\mu}{Pr} \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} \right) + \mu \left( \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)^2
\end{align}
</math>

where <math>Pr=c_{p_\infty}\mu_\infty/\kappa_\infty</math> is the [[Prandtl number]] with suffix <math>\infty</math> representing properties evaluated at infinity. The boundary conditions become

<math display="block"> u = v = h - h_w(x) = 0 \ \text{for} \ y=0,</math>
<math display="block"> u -U = h - h_\infty =0 \ \text{for} \ y=\infty \ \text{or} \ x=0.</math>

Unlike the incompressible boundary layer, similarity solution exists only if the transformation

<math display="block">x\rightarrow c^2 x, \quad y\rightarrow cy, \quad u\rightarrow u, \quad v\rightarrow \frac{v}{c}, \quad h\rightarrow h, \quad \rho\rightarrow \rho, \quad \mu\rightarrow \mu</math>

holds and this is possible only if <math>h_w=\text{constant}</math>.

===Howarth transformation===
[[File:CompBlasius.jpg|thumb|200x200px|Compressible Blasius boundary layer]]
Introducing the self-similar variables using [[Howarth–Dorodnitsyn transformation]]

<math display="block">\eta = \frac{U}{\sqrt{2 \rho_\infty \mu_\infty U x}} \int_0^y \rho \, dy, \quad f(\eta) = \frac{\psi}{\sqrt{2 \rho_\infty \mu_\infty U x}}, \quad \tilde h(\eta) = \frac{h}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde h_w = \frac{h_w}{h_\infty}, \quad \tilde \rho = \frac{\rho}{\rho_\infty}, \quad \tilde \mu = \frac{\mu}{\mu_\infty}</math>

the equations reduce to
<math display="block">\begin{align}
(\tilde\rho\tilde\mu f'')' + f f'' =0, \\
(\tilde\rho\tilde\mu \tilde h')' + Prf\tilde h' + Pr(\gamma-1)M^2 \tilde\rho\tilde\mu f''^2 =0 
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\gamma</math> is the [[specific heat ratio]] and <math>M=U/c_\infty</math> is the [[Mach number]], where <math>c_\infty</math> is the [[speed of sound]]. The equation can be solved once <math>\tilde \rho = \tilde \rho(\tilde h),\ \tilde \mu = \tilde \mu(\tilde h)</math> are specified. The boundary conditions are

<math display="block">f(0)=f'(0)=\theta(0)-\tilde h_w=f'(\infty)-1=\tilde h(\infty)-1=0.</math>

The commonly used expressions for air are <math>\gamma = 1.4, \ Pr = 0.7, \ \tilde\rho = \tilde h^{-1}, \ \tilde\mu = \tilde h^{2/3}</math>. If <math>c_p</math> is constant, then <math>\tilde h=\tilde \theta = T/T_\infty</math>. The temperature inside the boundary layer will increase even though the plate temperature is maintained at the same temperature as ambient, due to dissipative heating and of course, these dissipation effects are only pronounced when the [[Mach number]] <math>M</math> is large.

==First-order Blasius boundary layer in parabolic coordinates==

Since the boundary layer equations are [[Parabolic partial differential equation]], the natural coordinates for the problem is [[parabolic coordinates]].<ref name="VanDyke"/>{{rp|p=142}} The transformation from [[Cartesian coordinates]] <math>(x,y)</math> to [[parabolic coordinates]] <math>(\xi,\eta)</math> is given by

<math display="block">x + i y = \tfrac{1}{2} (\xi + i \eta)^2, \quad x = \tfrac{1}{2} (\xi^2-\eta^2), \quad y = \xi \eta. </math>
